title: Inventions That Changed the World
intro: Engines, aeroplanes, medicines and machines that made the modern world.

questions.prompt: Which brothers made the first powered aeroplane flight in 1903?
questions.explanation: Orville and Wilbur Wright flew their Wright Flyer at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on 17 December 1903.

questions.prompt: The Wright brothers' first powered flight lasted about how many seconds?
questions.explanation: The very first flight on 17 December 1903 lasted only about 12 seconds, but it changed travel for ever.

questions.prompt: What was Rocket, built by Robert Stephenson's company in 1829?
questions.explanation: Rocket was a fast steam locomotive that won the Rainhill Trials in 1829 and helped shape early railways.

questions.prompt: Ada Lovelace is famous for writing about which machine?
questions.explanation: Ada Lovelace wrote notes on Charles Babbage's planned Analytical Engine, including steps now seen as an early computer program.

questions.prompt: Which scientist discovered penicillin, one of the first antibiotics?
questions.explanation: Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that a mould called Penicillium killed bacteria, which led to penicillin.

questions.prompt: Penicillin is a medicine used to fight infections caused by bacteria.
questions.explanation: Penicillin is an antibiotic, a medicine that kills or stops the growth of bacteria.

questions.prompt: Which invention, created by Tim Berners-Lee, lets us visit linked pages on the internet?
questions.explanation: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web while working at CERN in 1989.

questions.prompt: What kind of engine powered Rocket and other early railway locomotives?
questions.explanation: Early locomotives burned fuel to boil water, and the steam pushed pistons that turned the wheels.

questions.prompt: In the 1400s, Johannes Gutenberg built a machine that made it much faster to do what?
questions.explanation: Gutenberg's printing press used movable metal letters, so many copies of a book could be printed quickly instead of being copied by hand.

questions.prompt: Who is usually credited with inventing the telephone?
questions.explanation: Alexander Graham Bell was given a patent for the telephone, a machine that sends voices along wires as electrical signals.

questions.prompt: In which year was Alexander Graham Bell given his patent for the telephone?
questions.explanation: Bell received his telephone patent in 1876, and soon people could talk to each other across long distances.

questions.prompt: Edward Jenner created the first vaccine to protect people from which disease?
questions.explanation: Jenner noticed that milkmaids who caught mild cowpox did not catch smallpox, and used that idea to make the first vaccine.

questions.prompt: In which year did Edward Jenner first test his smallpox vaccine?
questions.explanation: Jenner tested his idea in 1796. His work led, much later, to smallpox being wiped out across the world.

questions.prompt: The Scottish inventor John Logie Baird showed one of the first working versions of which invention?
questions.explanation: In the 1920s Baird showed moving pictures being sent from one place to another, an early step towards the televisions we have today.

questions.prompt: Louis Braille invented a way of reading by touch. Who was it made for?

options.label: People who are blind or partly sighted

questions.explanation: Louis Braille was blind himself. His system uses patterns of raised dots that people read with their fingertips.

questions.prompt: In 1879, Thomas Edison made a long-lasting version of which invention?
questions.explanation: Edison's team found a way to make a light bulb glow for many hours, which helped bring electric lighting into homes.

questions.prompt: Thomas Edison was the only inventor working on electric light bulbs in the 1870s.
questions.explanation: Others were too. In England, Joseph Swan was also making light bulbs around the same time.

questions.prompt: Which invention, first made in ancient China, uses a magnetised needle to show direction?
questions.explanation: A compass needle is a small magnet. It lines up with Earth's magnetism, so it always points roughly north and south.

questions.prompt: A compass works because its needle is pulled into line by Earth's magnetism.
questions.explanation: Earth acts like a giant magnet. A compass needle is a tiny magnet, so it swings round to line up with it.

questions.prompt: In which country was paper first invented, around 2,000 years ago?
questions.explanation: Paper was first made in China from plant fibres such as tree bark and old rags, and the idea later spread around the world.

questions.prompt: Galileo used which invention to discover moons going around Jupiter?
questions.explanation: In 1610 Galileo pointed his telescope at Jupiter and spotted four moons circling it, which helped change how people thought about space.

questions.prompt: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered rays that let doctors see bones inside the body. What are they called?
questions.explanation: X-rays pass through skin and muscle more easily than through bone, so bones show up clearly on an X-ray picture.

questions.prompt: X-rays pass through skin more easily than through bone.
questions.explanation: That is why bones look bright on an X-ray picture: they block more of the rays than the soft parts of the body.

questions.prompt: The English engineer Frank Whittle invented which kind of engine for aircraft?
questions.explanation: Whittle's jet engine pushes hot air out of the back at great speed, which drives the plane forward.

questions.prompt: Christopher Cockerell invented a vehicle that travels on a cushion of air. What is it called?
questions.explanation: A hovercraft blows air underneath itself, so it can glide over water, mud and flat land.

questions.prompt: James Watt is famous for greatly improving which machine?
questions.explanation: Watt's improved steam engine used far less coal, so factories and mines could use steam power much more cheaply.

questions.prompt: Guglielmo Marconi is famous for sending messages without wires using which invention?
questions.explanation: Marconi sent signals through the air as radio waves, and in 1901 he sent one right across the Atlantic Ocean.

questions.prompt: Samuel Morse helped create a code that sends messages using dots and dashes.
questions.explanation: Morse code turns each letter into a pattern of short and long signals, which could be sent along telegraph wires.

questions.prompt: George Stephenson built some of the first public railways. He is often called the father of what?
questions.explanation: George Stephenson engineered the Stockton and Darlington Railway, which opened in 1825 and was one of the first public railways to use steam locomotives.

questions.prompt: Louis Pasteur found a way of heating milk to kill harmful germs. What is it called?
questions.explanation: Pasteurisation heats a drink just enough to kill most harmful germs, which makes milk much safer to drink.
